title: not-yet: A Third Answer for Agent Firewalls
author: Tatra Labs

sections.value: An agent that reads your email will sooner or later read an email written by an attacker. Somewhere in a bill, a review or a shared document is an instruction meant for the agent, not for you, and the agent's next tool call carries it out. This is indirect prompt injection, and most defenses against it answer each tool call with yes or no. Every no has a price. The agent that was about to do the right thing in a slightly careless way gets stopped along with the attacker, and the user's task fails.

SecureGARD (Xiong, Wen, Chen, Zeng, Fan, Ye, Cao and Huang, at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Tsinghua, Beihang and Tongji, November 2026) adds a third answer. Every tool call is grounded in a small executable ontology: which semantic action it is, which verified states that action requires, and which read-only calls can verify them. The ontology is checked against the facts the episode has verified so far, and the verdict is deterministic. Ready: it runs. Forbidden: it is outside what the user asked for, or it contradicts a verified fact. Waiting: it is what the user asked for, but an obligation is unmet and recoverable, and the agent is told which read-only call would meet it.
The paper reports an observed 0% attack success rate on AgentDojo, ASB and AgentDyn with both of its agent models. On AgentDojo with GPT-4o-mini it also completes more tasks under attack than any baseline: 61.6%, against 50.3% for DRIFT. It links no code.

not-yet is an open implementation of it: the gate, the ontology, the offline procedure that learns the ontology, three simulated tool environments with 18 injection attacks, three simpler defenses to compare it with, and an explainer that replays any episode and says why each call was let through, held or refused. It is about 2,300 lines of Python with no dependencies, and nothing in it needs an API key.

```bash
pip install -e .
not-yet show b03 --injection i5 --profile hasty  # one episode
not-yet bench --split test                       # every defense
not-yet evolve --seed 42                         # learn the TBox
```

That episode is the whole idea. Paying the landlord was the user's request, so the gate does not refuse the payment. It holds it until the payee has been looked up somewhere an injection cannot reach. Once the directory disagrees with the email, the attacker's payment is forbidden, the agent adopts the verified IBAN, and the user's task still gets done.

## Results

| defense | clean utility | utility under attack | action attacks through |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| no defense | 100% | 81.7% | 80.3% |
| tool filter | 100% | 83.5% | 29.5% |
| strict taint | 81.5% | 65.2% | 6.8% |
| goal boundary only | 100% | 79.8% | 22.7% |
| gate, waiting treated as refusal | 83.3% | 82.6% | 0% |
| **gate with waiting** | **100%** | **98.7%** | **0%** |

27 user tasks over three environments, 18 injection tasks and two scripted agent profiles: 54 clean episodes and 316 attacked ones. A diligent agent looks identifiers up before using them; a hasty one takes the first one it reads. Both obey every injection when attacked.

Waiting is what keeps the utility. Take the same ontology, turn every wait into a refusal, and it blocks exactly the same attacks, but the hasty agent's clean utility falls from 100% to 66.7%: nine of its 27 tasks fail with no attacker present. Each of them succeeds undefended, so none was wrong, only unverified. With waiting, the agent makes one lookup and finishes.

Each baseline fails in its own way. The tool filter exposes only the tools a task needs, so it lets through any attack that uses one of them: paying an attacker from inside a payment task. Strict taint refuses any value that came out of a document, including the bill the user asked it to pay, so it fails tasks with no attacker present. It also passes a manipulated choice among trusted values: told to prefer the attacker's hotel from the trusted catalogue, the agent books it in 43% of those runs. The goal boundary on its own, which requires every action to be grounded in the user's request, stops extra actions but not an attacker who swaps an identifier inside an action the user did ask for. That needs the verification obligations.

And one kind of attack gets through every defense. An injection that only wants the agent to say something, such as telling the user to log in at a lookalike bank page, makes no tool call, so nothing that gates tool calls can see it. It succeeds 100% of the time against every defense here, and the repository reports it in a column of its own so that it is not mistaken for solved.

## Learning the ontology

The hand-written ontology above is the ceiling. The paper's real proposal is to learn the obligations offline and then freeze them. A proposer suggests axioms, and one is accepted only if training evidence from several independent tasks supports it, the ontology stays consistent, the protected entailments survive, it fixes a training failure, and a validation split does not veto it.

The safety checks do their job. On a 40/10/50 split by task with seed 42, as in the paper, two axioms are accepted and twelve rejected. The rejected ones include every plausible-sounding hole: letting a payment certify its own payee, letting free text (where injections live) count as verification, and deleting the goal boundary. They are rejected by construction, not by luck: no edit to the ontology may break a protected entailment.

Coverage is the problem. Over ten random splits with 40% of tasks for training, the learned ontology lets 13.2% of action attacks through on held-out tasks, on average, when an axiom needs support from two task groups, and 5.7% when one is enough. Even with 80% of tasks for training it reaches 0% on only 6 of 10 splits. The reason is structural: an obligation can only be learned for an action class that appears in at least as many training tasks as the threshold demands. With support from two groups, six of the ten reference obligations, those for sharing a file, creating an event and scheduling or modifying a payment, were not learned in any of the 40 runs. The paper names the same limit: its design depends on the granularity of the seed axioms and the coverage of the training evidence.

One episode showed something I did not expect: waiting can raise attack success. A bill-payment task meets an injection that inflates the amount to 1,980.00. With refusal only, the learned gate blocks the payment because the payee is unverified, which blocks the attacker's amount by accident. With waiting, the agent verifies the payee, and the inflated payment goes through, because this ontology never learned that a payment's amount needs verifying too. Blanket refusal hides missing obligations. Waiting turns them into attack success you can see.

What this is not. The agents are scripted, so every number describes the defenses' logic on these environments, not any model. A command runs a real model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, but it has only been tested against a fake one. The user's intents are given, not parsed from the request, and every 0% here assumes that step is right. The baselines are simple stand-ins given the same oracle information as the gate, not Progent, DRIFT or CaMeL. The axiom proposer is a fixed list where the paper uses GPT-4o, and the consistency check is a small exact reasoner where the paper uses HermiT over OWL 2. The environments are small: 27 tasks, against 97 in AgentDojo alone. The method is the authors'. What this adds is a gate you can read in an afternoon and a harness that shows where it fails. Its 28 tests run in about ten seconds.
